uniequip_002_makoto:
One afternoon, with the sun blazing overhead, Giada pointed at the warehouse before them, and Giulio and Makoto Yuki hauled the rolling shutter up together.
Inside it was cool enough. Giada walked to a certain row of storage shelves and said, "These are hers." She had Giulio go through everything on the table beside them, while Makoto stood at his side, helping to pack the items they decided to keep into a cardboard box.
"This is..." Giulio opened one storage box and sighed. "What an old song."
He asked Giada, "Are these all cassettes your aunt collected? Did you listen to them when you were going through her things?" Giada shook her head. "I didn't get through all of them... and not all of them are from her collection."
Giada picked out a few plain-looking ones and said, "These she must have recorded herself. I mentioned to Makoto that I'd heard a song among her effects—it was here." Makoto looked slightly puzzled; Giulio asked curiously, "Which one? I want to hear it too."
Giada hesitated, then took out a cassette, put it into the radio beside her, plugged it in, and pressed play.
The home-recorded tape hissed. With no accompaniment, a slightly husky woman's voice sang something tender and full of longing—and Giulio slowly found himself close to tears. The afternoon sun reached into the warehouse, and the dazzling white light lay across the floor like ripples of water.
"...Sugar and guns and faith, I drink Laterano down in one." He sang the last few lines along with her, under his breath.
The music ended, and the first to speak was, surprisingly, Makoto. "I remember now—what Giada said back then... So your insistence about the funeral had to do with this song?"
Giada said, "...Yes. This tape must have been recorded not long ago... Though taking the feeling I got from one song and treating it as the deceased's wish was still presumptuous of me."
Makoto shook his head. "Music really can tell us a great deal."
"...Come to think of it, Makoto listens to music often, doesn't he?" Giulio ducked his head to wipe his eyes, then recovered his usual smile.
"Not especially..." With the subject suddenly turned on him, Makoto was caught off guard, and Giada quietly let out a breath. Giulio pressed on, "What do you usually listen to, Makoto?"
"...These. You can listen too." Makoto switched on the player he always carried and showed it to them.
"Actually, isn't listening to the same song a bit like empathy?" Giulio said suddenly, rubbing his chin.
"No one here but you knows what empathy feels like..." Giada couldn't help saying.
"...I think I understand it." Makoto answered in earnest all the same.
Something came back to Giada then. That day, that one evening, what she had felt. At the very end, she had certainly heard music—the sound of a cello, like starlight, like the glow of dusk.
"...Then perhaps I have felt it too," Giada said.
"Right? Music is a feeling you can hear." Giulio smiled gently.
"There has always been a way to feel what someone else feels." Makoto looked at Giulio and said seriously, "There are a great many things that can tie us together."
"If such a moment ever existed, then it will never disappear," he said.
